title: Heap Sort
definition: Heap Sort is an efficient comparison-based sorting algorithm that uses a binary heap data structure. It first builds a max heap (or min heap) from the input data, then repeatedly extracts the maximum (or minimum) element from the heap and rebuilds the heap until all elements are sorted.
conceptExplanation: Heap Sort works in two phases: 1) Build a max heap from the array, where the largest element is at the root. 2) Repeatedly swap the root (maximum) with the last element of the heap, reduce the heap size by one, and heapify the root to restore the max heap property. After n-1 extractions, the array is sorted in ascending order. Uses either a max heap (for ascending sort) or min heap (for descending sort).
keyPoints: - Binary heap structure - Two phases: build heap and extract - O(n log n) time complexity - In-place sort (except for heap size tracking) - Not stable
importantTerminology: Heap Sort, Binary Heap, Max Heap, Min Heap, Heapify, Root, Last element
workingPrinciple:
Phase 1: Build a max heap from the input array. The build-heap operation starts from the last non-leaf node (index floor(n/2)-1) and heapifies each node moving upward to the root. This ensures the largest element is at index 0.

Phase 2: Swap the root (arr[0], the maximum) with the last element of the heap (arr[n-1]). Reduce the conceptual heap size by 1 (the last element is now in its final sorted position). Call heapify on the root (index 0) with the reduced heap size. Repeat this extraction n-1 times. After each extraction, the next largest element moves to its correct position at the end of the array.
realLifeExample: Priority queue sorting, situations requiring guaranteed O(n log n) with minimal memory
diagram: Heap sort steps: Build max heap [13, 11, 12, 5, 6, 7] → swap root 13 with last 7 → [7, 11, 12, 5, 6, 13] (13 sorted, ignore last) → heapify root: 7→ children 11,12 → swap with 12 → [12, 11, 7, 5, 6, 13] → swap root 12 with last 6 → [6, 11, 7, 5, 12, 13] (12 sorted) → heapify → ... → [5, 6, 7, 11, 12, 13] sorted
algorithm:
Heap Sort Algorithm:
1. BUILD-MAX-HEAP(arr)
2. FOR i = n DOWNTO 2
3.   SWAP arr[1] WITH arr[i]  (swap root with last element)
4.   HEAP-SIZE = HEAP-SIZE - 1
5.   MAX-HEAPIFY(arr, 1)
6. END FOR

BUILD-MAX-HEAP(arr):
1. SET heap-size = n
2. FOR i = floor(n/2) DOWNTO 1
3.   MAX-HEAPIFY(arr, i)

MAX-HEAPIFY(arr, i):
1. SET l = 2*i (left child)
2. SET r = 2*i + 1 (right child)
3. LARGEST = i
4. IF l <= heap-size AND arr[l] > arr[LARGEST]
5.   SET LARGEST = l
6. END IF
7. IF r <= heap-size AND arr[r] > arr[LARGEST]
8.   SET LARGEST = r
9. END IF
10. IF LARGEST != i
11.   SWAP arr[i] WITH arr[LARGEST]
12.   MAX-HEAPIFY(arr, LARGEST)
13. END IF

NOTE: This uses 1-based indexing notation. In code, use 0-based: left = 2*i + 1, right = 2*i + 2.
pseudocode:
BEGIN
  // Build max heap\n  FUNCTION buildMaxHeap(arr)
    SET n = length(arr)
    FOR i = floor(n/2) DOWNTO 1
      maxHeapify(arr, i)
    END FOR
  END FUNCTION

  // Heapify subtree rooted at i\n  FUNCTION maxHeapify(arr, i)
    SET l = 2*i
    SET r = 2*i + 1
    SET largest = i
    IF l <= heap-size AND arr[l] > arr[largest]
      SET largest = l
    END IF
    IF r <= heap-size AND arr[r] > arr[largest]
      SET largest = r
    END IF
    IF largest != i
      SWAP arr[i] WITH arr[largest]
      maxHeapify(arr, largest)
    END IF
  END FUNCTION

  // Heap sort\n  FUNCTION heapSort(arr)
    buildMaxHeap(arr)
    FOR i = length(arr) DOWNTO 2
      SWAP arr[1] WITH arr[i]
      SET heap-size = heap-size - 1
      maxHeapify(arr, 1)
    END FOR
    RETURN arr
  END FUNCTION
END
complexity:
Time: Always O(n log n) - best, average, and worst case\nSpace: O(1) - in-place sort (no extra array needed)\n
Heapify is O(log n), build-heap is O(n), extraction is O(n log n)

Note: Build-heap can be done in O(n), not O(n log n) as naive analysis
applications: When guaranteed O(n log n) is needed with minimal memory, embedded systems, priority queue operations
advantages: O(n log n) guaranteed time complexity, in-place O(1) space, no recursive stack overflow (can be implemented iteratively)
limitations: Not stable, larger constant factor than quick sort in practice, more complex to understand and implement than simple sorts
commonMistakes: Incorrect heapify logic (comparing wrong indices), off-by-one in left/right child calculation (0-based: 2i+1, 2i+2), not reducing heap size after extraction, forgetting to call heapify after swap
importantExamPoints:
Build-heap: starts from floor(n/2)-1 upward, O(n) not O(n log n)
0-based indexing: left child = 2*i + 1, right child = 2*i + 2
Heap sort is in-place (O(1) extra space), not stable
Always O(n log n) time - no worst case like quick sort
Three-way heap sort variations: bottom-up and top-down

Bottom-up heap sort: builds heap from leaves upward (more efficient)\nTop-down heap sort: inserts elements one by one (like binary search tree)\n
Practical note: Used when O(1) space is required and stability is not needed.

fiveMarkQuestions.question: Explain heap sort algorithm and complexity analysis.
fiveMarkQuestions.answer:
Heap Sort uses a binary heap data structure. It has two phases:

Phase 1 - Build Max Heap: Start from the last non-leaf node (index floor(n/2)-1 in 0-based) and call heapify on each node moving upward to the root. This ensures the largest element is at the root (index 0). Build-heap operation is O(n), not O(n log n) as the naive analysis suggests.

Phase 2 - Extract Elements: Swap the root (maximum element) with the last element of the heap. Reduce the heap size by 1 (the last element is now in its final sorted position). Call heapify on the root to restore the max heap property. Repeat this n-1 times.

Complexity:
- Time: Always O(n log n) for best, average, and worst case
- Build-heap: O(n)
- Extraction phase: O(n log n) total (each of n-1 heapify operations is O(log n))
- Space: O(1) - in-place, no extra array needed
- Build-heap can be optimized to O(n) using the sift-down method from bottom up

Heapify: Recursively ensures the subtree rooted at index i satisfies the max heap property. Compare with left and right children, swap if necessary, and continue down the heap.

Not stable: Equal elements may change relative order during heapify and extraction.

Applications: When guaranteed O(n log n) with O(1) space is needed. Priority queue implementation. Embedded systems.

Comparison: vs Merge Sort: heap sort in-place O(1) vs merge sort O(n) space. merge sort stable, heap sort not. vs Quick Sort: heap sort guaranteed O(n log n) vs quick sort worst O(n²). Quick sort typically faster in practice due to cache efficiency.

Space: O(1) - in-place sort

tenMarkQuestions.question: Explain heap sort with algorithm, heap property, build-heap, and complexity.
tenMarkQuestions.answer:
Heap Sort: 

Algorithm: Uses a binary heap data structure. Two phases:

1. Build-heap: Convert the array into a max heap (for ascending sort). Start from the last non-leaf node at index floor(n/2) - 1 (0-based) and call maxHeapify on each node moving upward to the root. After this phase, arr[0] contains the largest element.

2. Extraction: Swap arr[0] (root/maximum) with arr[i] (last unsorted element). Reduce the conceptual heap size by 1 (i is now sorted). Call maxHeapify on the root (index 0) with the reduced heap size. Repeat for i = n-1 down to 1.

Heap Property: In a max heap, arr[i] >= arr[2*i+1] and arr[i] >= arr[2*i+2] for all i. The largest element is at the root.

0-based Indexing: Left child of i = 2*i + 1, Right child of i = 2*i + 2, Parent of i = floor((i-1)/2)

Complexity:
- Time: Θ(n log n) for all cases (best, average, worst)
- Build-heap: O(n) - can be proven by analyzing the height of nodes
- Extraction: (n-1) calls to heapify, each O(log n), total O(n log n)
- Space: O(1) in-place
- Total comparisons: ~2n log n + O(n)

Heapify Algorithm: 
1. Assume subtree at index i is almost a max heap, but arr[i] might be smaller than its children
2. Find largest among i, left child (2i+1), right child (2i+2)
3. If largest != i, swap arr[i] with arr[largest] and recursively heapify the affected subtree

Comparison with Other Sorts:
- vs Merge Sort: Heap sort in-place O(1) space, merge sort O(n) space. Merge sort stable, heap sort not stable. Both O(n log n) time.
- vs Quick Sort: Both O(n log n) average, but heap sort guaranteed no worst case O(n²). Quick sort typically 2-3x faster in practice due to cache locality.
- vs Insertion/Bubble/Selection: O(n log n) vs O(n²), much faster for large data.

Practical Note: Heap sort is useful when memory is constrained (O(1) extra) and stability is not required. Often used for priority queue operations.
